title: Phase 4 — Plant Disease Classification Across Image Datasets
timing_note: Provisional ~9-minute version including demo; duration and dates must be confirmed. Slides 11–12 are backup.

slides.title:
Plant disease classification
across image datasets
slides.subtitle:
Does a model trained on one image collection
still work on another?
slides.notes: Our project asks whether a plant disease classifier can handle images beyond the collection it learned from. We compared two ways of adapting the same lightweight model. The experiment is complete; this presentation explains our measured results, including where the models fail. The main finding is a large drop on the second dataset, not a claim that we solved plant diagnosis.

slides.title: The practical problem
slides.subtitle: Casual plant photos vary. A familiar-looking test can hide that challenge.
cards: Casual gardeners and plant owners taking everyday photographs.
A confident wrong label can send someone in the wrong direction.
Does fine-tuning help a lightweight model transfer between datasets?
slides.notes: A gardener will not necessarily control lighting, framing, or background. This motivates evaluating a classifier on a different image collection. We are investigating robustness, not promising it. Comparing two datasets does not isolate weather or photography skill as causes. This is a research comparison; we did not build a diagnostic service.

slides.title: Two collections, one shared label set
slides.subtitle: A label means the plant condition written in the dataset annotation.
cards: Training images and same-dataset testing. Mostly controlled leaf photographs.
Separate testing on internet-sourced photographs with different image conditions.
Healthy leaves and named conditions. Five uncertain category pairs excluded.
slides.source: Paper: Methods, Tables I–II; configs/categories.json; PlantDoc [1].
slides.notes: PlantVillage is the source collection: the one we trained on. Cropped PlantDoc is the target collection: the different one used for external testing. We matched 22 plant-condition categories and excluded five uncertain pairs rather than assume similar names meant identical conditions. These labels are dataset annotations, not diagnoses independently verified by us. Cropped PlantDoc is also not a controlled sample of future users.

slides.title: Keep learning separate from testing
slides.subtitle: The same image lists were used for both model versions and all three seeds.
slides.source: Paper: Methods, Table I; fixed splits; selected-checkpoints.json.
slides.notes: Training fits the model weights. Validation selects the saved checkpoint with the lowest prediction loss, without using the final tests. The two test sets answer different questions: familiar collection versus different collection. We grouped known photos of the same leaf and checked identical files to reduce overlap. Some related or altered duplicates may still escape these checks. PlantDoc test results did not select models or training settings. The first two boxes describe development; the last two are separate final evaluations, not additional training stages.

slides.title: Same starting model. Different learning.
slides.subtitle: MobileNetV3-Small, pretrained on ImageNet; a new layer predicts 22 categories.
cards:
Keep earlier image features fixed.
Train only the final category layer.

Warm up the category layer for one epoch.
Then also train the earlier features.
slides.bottom: Three seeds · fixed splits · no random augmentation in this experiment
slides.notes: Pretrained means the model already learned image patterns on ImageNet before our plant experiment. The frozen baseline reuses these patterns unchanged and only learns the final category layer. Fine-tuning also adjusts the earlier feature weights after one warmup epoch. We replaced the entire original classifier with one linear 576-to-22 layer. Batch-normalization running statistics stayed fixed in both versions. Three seeds repeat training with different initial category weights and image order, using the same split. Maximum ten epochs, AdamW, and source-validation early stopping were fixed. No random augmentation was used for the published experiment; later optional code does not change that.

slides.title: Strong source scores did not transfer
slides.subtitle: Fine-tuning helped on PlantDoc, but the cross-dataset gap remained large.
slides.source: Original final results: three seeds; 5,487 source / 183 target images. Error bars: seed SD.
slides.notes: Frozen-feature mean accuracy was 97.59 percent on PlantVillage and 21.68 percent on PlantDoc. Fine-tuned accuracy was 99.07 and 25.87 percent respectively. The PlantDoc improvement was 4.19 percentage points, not 4.19 percent relative improvement. Macro-F1, which gives each category equal weight, shows the same broad pattern. Error bars describe variation between three training seeds on the same test images; they are not confidence intervals for new photographs. We report every seed, not just the best run.

slides.title: A recurring mistake worth investigating
slides.subtitle: The models often predicted “tomato late blight” on the PlantDoc test set.
cards: Frozen models predicted that label across the three separate runs.
Fine-tuned models predicted that label across the three separate runs.
slides.source: Paper: Results; docs/evaluation/final-results.json. Each run tests the same 183 images.
slides.notes: This is one error pattern from the full evaluation, not just our demo examples. Ten of the 183 target images were annotated as tomato late blight. The frozen models predicted that label 61, 70, and 75 times; the fine-tuned models predicted it 59, 54, and 42 times. This identifies a behavior to investigate. It does not tell us the visual or biological cause, and it does not justify changing the dataset labels simply because the model disagrees.

slides.title: What these results cannot establish
slides.subtitle: The limits are part of the finding.
cards: 183 images; only 3–12 examples per category. Three seeds reuse those images.
Category matching and duplicate checks reduce known problems, not every problem.
Background, lighting, framing and labels change together. Weather and skill were not isolated.
slides.notes: We evaluated one architecture, one split and one fixed training configuration. The target test set is small and internet-sourced. We cannot claim general field accuracy or statistical significance from three training seeds. Our uncertainty is not solved by counting each repeated prediction as a new test photograph. The domain shift includes many simultaneous differences, so we cannot attribute the accuracy drop to weather, camera skills or any single cause.

slides.title: High familiar-image accuracy is not enough.
slides.subtitle: External evaluation changed the story.
cards: A reproducible frozen-versus-fine-tuned comparison with all planned seeds.
Fine-tuning helped modestly. Reliable cross-dataset performance was not demonstrated.
slides.bottom: Next: separate augmentation/adaptation studies and a larger checked external test set.
slides.source: Existing IEEE paper and measured results are linked from the repository README.
slides.notes: Our contribution is an empirical baseline and reproducibility exercise, not a new architecture or the first study of this dataset shift. We completed the agreed comparison and found a clear gap. Future augmentation or adaptation experiments need their own records and evaluation plan. We should not tune against these already observed test scores and call that a new unseen test. The code, paper, plots and detailed measurements are available in the repository. Invite questions.

slides.title: Backup: how someone can repeat the work
slides.subtitle: The paper describes the original code snapshot, 9619975.
cards: Pinned dataset versions → image audit → fixed splits → three training pairs → verification → tests.
Demo uses the saved original pair. A fresh clone needs data and models; the offline replay is a local backup.
slides.notes: Use this slide only for questions. The original saved checkpoints are fingerprinted and require the original code; the demo loads verified historical modules automatically. Full reproduction uses a separate worktree at 9619975 so optional later training changes do not get mixed into the paper. Raw images, models and private notes are not on GitHub. Reproduction commands generate separate records; exact numerical equality across different devices is not guaranteed.
